PMGT1852 Week 10

PMGT1852 Week 10 - The Secrets to Focusing: Checkpoints, PeDeQs and Breakout Groups

Overview

Once the session is running, the facilitator keeps every agenda item clear and on track. This week covers:

• The checkpoint at the start of every agenda item: review, preview, big view.

• The extended checkpoint used when restarting the session (for example after a break).

• Pre-questions that warm up the group before the real question.

• PeDeQs: the six parts of a clear, accurate, concise instruction.

• Staying on track with Label, Prompt, Redirect.

• Breakout groups: the "do, divide, direct" principle, the seven steps, and peer review of each other's work.

Key Concepts

Checkpoint

At the start of every agenda item or facilitation process, give a checkpoint with three parts:

• Review - a quick recap of what has been completed so far.

• Preview - a short description of what the group will do next.

• Big view - how this item serves the overall goal of the meeting.

The checkpoint signals to everyone that a transition is happening. The big view tells participants why this step deserves their time, always linking back to the meeting goal; it plays the same role as Excite in the opening.

Extended checkpoint

When the session restarts - after a break, for example - use an extended checkpoint: remind the group of the overall meeting goal, review all agenda items completed so far, preview all items still to come, and explain how the remaining items relate to the overall goal.

Pre-questions (warming up the group)

Before asking the real question, ask two pre-questions that require a non-verbal response (a raised hand or a nod). They get people responding, so that when the real question comes, hands go up more readily.

Frameworks and Formulas

PeDeQs: six parts of an instruction

Step

Content

1 Purpose

The purpose of the activity

2 Example

A simple example, where appropriate

3 Directions

General directions, using word pictures and gestures

4 Exceptions

Specific exceptions and special cases

5 Questions

Asking whether there are any questions

6 Starting question

A question that lets participants begin formulating answers

Memory aid: PeDeQs = Purpose-Example, Directions-Exceptions, Questions-Starting question.

Why PeDeQs: clear instructions empower participants. They explain what to do, why, and how, and prevent confusion and interruptions later.

Tips: prepare the directions before the meeting; ask yourself "Where might someone be confused?"; after the purpose, give an example or analogy that is unrelated to the meeting content (the classic example is a turkey dinner); word the starting question carefully.

The starting question launches the activity and steers thinking, but it cannot replace the directions - both are needed.

Label, Prompt, Redirect (keeping the group on track)

• Label - give every chart the title of the agenda item it belongs to.

• Prompt - ask extended prompt questions ("What else?", "What other steps are there in the hiring process?").

• Redirect - monitor relevance; if the group goes off track, ask a redirection question with the group's agreement rather than cutting people off.

Breakout groups

Use breakout groups when the agenda requires a facilitation process to be run several times.

Principle: do, divide, direct - do the first one together with the whole group, then divide into groups, then give the final directions.

The seven steps:

Tell participants they will be split into groups.

Complete the first element with the whole group.

Split into groups.

Appoint team leaders, scribes and reporters.

Give the final directions.

Monitor the groups.

Have each group report its results.

Grouping: 3-7 people per group. Choose the grouping method according to the goal - speed, mixing people up, diversity, or putting domain enthusiasts together.

The final directions must state: the deliverable, how its quality will be judged, the process for producing it, and the deadline.

Peer review of team work: rotate each group's flip chart to another group for review - an efficient way to get high-quality feedback. The reviewing group focuses on how to improve the other group's content.

Worked Examples

A checkpoint for the hiring-process case

"We have just completed the getting started segment [review; tick it on the agenda chart]. Our next step is to identify how the hiring process works today [preview]. This matters because once we identify all the steps we can see where problems occur and how to make it a much better process [big view]."

What happens without a big view

The facilitator announces the move to the "current process" step without giving a reason. A participant objects: the task force exists to build a new process, so discussing the old one is a waste of time. The facilitator ends up defending the agenda item.

The consequences: participants resist the item; a big view given afterwards sounds like self-justification; tension is created; and the outspoken participant is embarrassed. Giving the big view first lets participants understand why the item is worth discussing.

Pre-questions in action

"How many have been involved with a project that wasn't well planned? (raises hand) It was difficult, wasn't it? (nods) ... So there are real benefits to planning, aren't there? (nods) What are the benefits of planning? Who can tell me one? (raises hand)"

The two warm-up questions take only hand raises and nods; by the third question the group is already responding.

PeDeQs applied: a full instruction (hiring process)

• Purpose: to identify problems, symptoms and root causes in one table.

• Example (unrelated to the meeting content): a turkey dinner - the problem is "burnt turkey", the symptom is "turkey black", and the root causes are cooked too long, oven too hot, broken thermometer, a bad cook.

• Directions: first list all the problems with the hiring process; then, for each problem, identify the symptom and the root cause.

• Exceptions: if a root cause appears early, put it in the root-cause column until its problem is found; problems discovered later are added at the bottom.

• Questions: "Any questions?"

• Starting question: "Think about the last time you hired someone ... the things that made you say 'We've got to fix this process' ... What problems are there with the hiring process?"

Redirecting with agreement

The group is listing process steps when Carl raises the question of the process's total duration. The facilitator acknowledges that it is an issue that must be handled and asks: "Is it OK if we put it on the Issues list ... and then see if there are any other steps we still need to list?" Carl agrees. The topic is parked, not lost, and the group continues.

Building a PeDeQs instruction for a new activity

Suppose the activity is to collect one stakeholder concern to guide later engagement:

• Purpose: identify the concerns that should shape the work.

• Example: show one concrete concern (for example, regional students struggling with file transfers).

• Directions: each participant names one group of people affected and one concern; concerns that cannot yet be substantiated are marked as items to verify rather than treated as evidence.

• Exceptions: none needed for a short activity.

• Questions: check that the directions are understood.

• Starting question: "Which stakeholder concern should we consider first?"
